questions.stem: Choose the correct tense: 'By the time I ______ home, she had already left.'

options.option_text: reach (wrong: 'by the time I reach' + 'had left' is incorrect; 'reach' (present) with 'had left' (past perfect) is inconsistent)
reached (correct: 'By the time I REACHED home' (simple past) + 'she had already left' (past perfect for earlier event) ✓)
had reached (wrong: 'by the time I had reached' double past perfect is unusual and non-standard here)
was reaching (wrong: 'by the time' + past continuous doesn't match the past perfect in the result clause)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'BY THE TIME + simple past (reached), + past perfect (had left).' Rule: when 'by the time' refers to a past situation, the main clause uses past perfect (had + V3) and the 'by the time' clause uses simple past.

questions.stem: Choose the correct tense: 'I ______ this book for the past three hours.'

options.option_text: read (wrong: 'read' = simple past; doesn't show ongoing action for three hours)
have been reading (correct: present perfect continuous for action ongoing from past to now for a duration ✓)
am reading (wrong: present continuous doesn't show the three-hour duration)
was reading (wrong: past continuous for ongoing past action; 'for three hours' here implies still ongoing)

questions.explanation: B is correct. PRESENT PERFECT CONTINUOUS = have/has been + V-ing. Used for actions that started in the past and CONTINUE TO THE PRESENT, especially with durations like 'for three hours,' 'since morning.' 'I HAVE BEEN READING this book for the past three hours' (and still am).

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'Look! The cat ______ up the tree.'

options.option_text: climbs (wrong: present simple for habits/facts; 'look!' signals something happening NOW)
is climbing (correct: 'Look!' = draw attention to something happening RIGHT NOW → present continuous ✓)
climbed (wrong: past tense for completed action; but it's happening now)
has climbed (wrong: present perfect for recently completed action; but the cat is actively doing it now)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Look!' is a signal that something is happening RIGHT NOW → Present Continuous. 'Look! The cat IS CLIMBING up the tree.' Other 'happening now' signals: listen!, watch!, here comes...!, can you see...?

questions.stem: Choose the correct tense: 'She ______ this company since 2010.'

options.option_text: works for (wrong: present simple doesn't indicate the ongoing period since 2010)
has worked for (correct: present perfect with 'since' for an action from past continuing to present ✓)
worked for (wrong: past simple = completed action; but she still works there)
had worked for (wrong: past perfect = before another past action; not appropriate here)

questions.explanation: B is correct. SINCE + year/point of time → use PRESENT PERFECT (has/have + V3) for ongoing situations. 'She HAS WORKED for this company since 2010' = started in 2010 and still works there. Compare: 'She WORKED for the company for 10 years' (and no longer does) = simple past.

questions.stem: Choose the correct tense: 'If I ______ a millionaire, I would travel the world.'

options.option_text: am (wrong: 'am' + 'would travel' = mixed tenses; 'am' is present, 'would' is conditional)
were (correct: Type 2 conditional for hypothetical: 'If I WERE + would' (including 'if I were' even with first/second person) ✓)
will be (wrong: 'if I will be' — never use 'will' in the 'if' clause)
have been (wrong: 'have been' introduces an unrelated tense; Type 2 needs simple past in 'if' clause)

questions.explanation: B is correct. TYPE 2 CONDITIONAL (hypothetical present/future): If + past simple/were, would + base verb. For 'to be,' use 'WERE' (not 'was') for all persons in formal English: 'If I WERE a millionaire.' This is the subjunctive mood. 'If I was' is acceptable in informal speech.

questions.stem: Choose the correct tense: 'I ______ you if I had known you were in trouble.'

options.option_text: would help (wrong: 'would help' = Type 2; but 'had known' = past perfect → Type 3 conditional)
would have helped (correct: Type 3 conditional for impossible past: would have + V3 in result clause ✓)
will help (wrong: 'will help' = future simple; doesn't match the past perfect in 'if' clause)
help (wrong: bare infinitive doesn't work in Type 3 conditional)

questions.explanation: B is correct. TYPE 3 CONDITIONAL (impossible past, regret): If + past perfect (had known), would have + V3 (would have helped). 'I WOULD HAVE HELPED you if I had known...' = I didn't help because I didn't know. Past condition, past hypothetical result.

questions.stem: Choose the correct tense: 'We ______ this project by next Monday.'

options.option_text: will finish (wrong: 'will finish' = future simple; doesn't emphasise completion by a deadline)
will have finished (correct: future perfect = action completed by a specific future time ✓)
finish (wrong: present simple for future; used with timetable sense only)
will be finishing (wrong: future continuous = ongoing action at a future time; not completion)

questions.explanation: B is correct. FUTURE PERFECT = will have + V3. Used for actions that will be completed BEFORE a specific future time/event. 'We WILL HAVE FINISHED this project BY next Monday' = by the deadline, the project will already be done.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses PAST PERFECT CONTINUOUS correctly?

options.option_text: She had been waiting for two hours when the train finally arrived. (correct: had been + V-ing = past perfect continuous; shows how long before another past event ✓)
She has been waiting for two hours. (wrong: 'has been' = present perfect continuous; not past perfect continuous)
She was waiting for two hours when the train arrived. (wrong: 'was waiting' = past continuous; not past perfect continuous)
She had waited for two hours when the train arrived. (wrong: 'had waited' = past perfect simple; not continuous)

questions.explanation: A is correct. PAST PERFECT CONTINUOUS = had been + V-ing. Shows: an action that was ongoing for a period BEFORE another past event occurred. 'She HAD BEEN WAITING for two hours WHEN the train arrived.' The waiting lasted until the train's arrival.

questions.stem: Identify the tense used: 'He will be sleeping at midnight.'

options.option_text: Future Simple (will + V1 — but the sentence uses 'be + sleeping')
Future Continuous (correct: will be + V-ing = future continuous; action ongoing at a future time ✓)
Future Perfect (will have + V3 — but the sentence uses 'be sleeping', not 'have slept')
Present Continuous (is/am/are + V-ing — but sentence uses 'will be')

questions.explanation: B is correct. FUTURE CONTINUOUS = will be + V-ing. 'He WILL BE SLEEPING at midnight' = at midnight (future time), he will be in the middle of sleeping (ongoing). Compare: Future Simple 'He will sleep at midnight' (he will start sleeping at midnight); Future Continuous (he will already be asleep at midnight).

questions.stem: Choose the correct tense for a historical fact: 'The Indian Constitution ______ on 26 January 1950.'

options.option_text: came into effect (correct: simple past for specific past events ✓)
has come into effect (wrong: present perfect with specific past dates (26 January 1950) is incorrect)
comes into effect (wrong: present simple for future/schedules; not historical facts)
had come into effect (wrong: past perfect for earlier-than-another-past event; here there's no second past event mentioned)

questions.explanation: A is correct. SIMPLE PAST is used for historical events with specific dates: 'The Indian Constitution CAME INTO EFFECT on 26 January 1950.' When a specific past date is mentioned ('on 26 January 1950'), always use simple past — never present perfect ('has come into effect').
